archetype.name: Pocket Passer (intermediate attack)
archetype.definition: A tall, rhythm-based thrower who now wins mostly from the pocket, living on throws in the 10-to-19-yard window off a balanced, under-center-friendly offense rather than on his legs or volume.

report.headline: The intermediate game made Lawrence a top-five efficiency passer; the TD rate won't last.
report.take:
Lawrence has never had a season that looks like this. Across five prior years his best completion-over-expected was 1.4 (2022), and last year he sat at -1.9 with a 13.9% bad-throw rate. This year he is at +4.76 CPOE, his bad-throw rate has fallen to 9.8% (5th of 42), and his 0.303 EPA per dropback ranks 4th of 49 against a league average near zero. He is getting the ball out a bit quicker (2.72 seconds, down 0.15) and taking slightly fewer tight-window throws, and the result is the cleanest version of him we have seen. He is also running far less: 9.9 rushing yards a game against 21.1 last year, with only eight designed runs. This is a pocket passer now.

The engine is one area of the field. On 68 attempts between 10 and 19 air yards he is at 0.748 EPA per attempt with a +8.9 CPOE, and those throws alone account for 50.9 of his 68.7 dropback EPA. Add the 23 deep shots (1.114 per attempt, +14.2 CPOE) and his 10-plus-yard throws carry the offense while the short game is merely solid (0.18 per attempt) and the screens and swings behind the line are a wash. The middle of the field is where it peaks (0.725 EPA per attempt), and so does the under-center work: 0.523 EPA per play with a +10.2 CPOE, against 0.216 from shotgun. That reads as a Coen design. Under-center looks and intermediate in-breakers create defined, open throws, and Lawrence is finally hitting them consistently.

The headline numbers also flatter him in two ways. First, 18 touchdowns on 224 attempts is an 8% TD rate (2nd of 49), almost double the league's 4.3%. In the red zone he is completing just 48.8% with a -4.3 CPOE yet has 10 scores there, a mix that rarely holds. Second, the volume is modest by design. He averages 28 attempts, the team passes slightly less than situation predicts, and a defense ranked 3rd in EPA keeps handing him leads. His yardage rank (15th) lags his efficiency ranks for that reason. His weaker spots are the high-leverage ones: a 38.3% third-down conversion rate with three of his four interceptions on third down, and a 0.367 success rate in close fourth quarters.

The recent path is mixed. Over the last three games his EPA per dropback is up to 0.356 and his yards per attempt is up to 9.36, but his CPOE has slid to -0.1, with negative marks in three of the last four games. The explosive plays are still coming. The pinpoint accuracy that defined September has cooled, and the gains lean more on yards after the catch and scheme. Expect him to stay a top-tier efficiency passer with a capped volume ceiling, and expect the touchdown count to come back toward something like last season's rate.

strengths.title: Owns the 10-to-19-yard window
strengths.body: His intermediate throws produce most of his value, at a success rate of 66% and well above expected completion. Throws of 10-plus air yards as a group carry a +10.2 CPOE, and the deep ball has been both accurate and explosive. This is a skill change, not one hot game: it held up across opponents and lines up with the drop in his bad-throw rate. The deep split is only 23 attempts, so that piece will cool somewhat, but the intermediate base is large enough to trust.

strengths.title: Ball placement finally cleaned up
strengths.body: For most of his career, erratic placement was his flaw: bad-throw rates of 18-20% in 2021 and 2023 and interception totals ranked near the bottom of the league. This year his bad-throw rate is down 4.1 points from last season and ranks 5th, and his interception rate is better than the league average. A quicker clock and slightly less forcing into tight windows explain part of it. Because it shows up in charting and not just in luck, it should mostly hold, though his three turnover-worthy fumbles are a reminder that he is not mistake-free.

strengths.title: Under-center game punishes defenses
strengths.body: When he is under center, his EPA per play more than doubles his shotgun mark and his CPOE jumps to +10.2. That points to play-action and defined reads built by the scheme, which suit a tall, rhythm passer. It is a 52-play sample, but it fits the team's 5th-ranked passing EPA and a run game that is efficient enough to sell the fakes.

concerns.title: Touchdown rate is running hot
concerns.body: An 8% TD rate is nearly double the league average and far above anything in his career. Last year's 29 touchdowns came at 1.71 a game; he is at 2.25 now. His red-zone completion rate is under 50% with a negative CPOE, yet he has 10 red-zone scores. That is a finishing rate that tends to settle. The efficiency is real, but the touchdown count is the most likely number to come down.

concerns.title: Accuracy has cooled lately
concerns.body: His CPOE over the last three games is -0.1, nearly five points below his season mark, and Week 9 was -5.4 even in a blowout win. Yards per attempt and EPA rose over the same stretch, so explosive plays and YAC are covering for it for now. If the placement slips back toward his 2024-25 levels, the efficiency will follow, so this is the thing to monitor rather than a verdict yet.

concerns.title: Money downs lag the rest
concerns.body: He converts only 38.3% of third downs, facing an average of 8.7 yards to go, and three of his four picks came there. In close fourth quarters his success rate drops to 0.367 with a -7 CPOE. Long third downs are hard for everyone, and close late snaps have been rare because of the defense, so part of this is context and small samples. Still, it is the one area where the old, looser version of him shows through.

trend.note: After the Week 2 dud at Denver (-4.1 EPA), he has had positive passing EPA every week, and his last three games are his most efficient stretch by EPA per dropback and adjusted net yards. The caveat is that CPOE has turned negative over that same run.

nextGame.headline: A leaky Titans secondary, but a blowout script could cap volume
nextGame.body:
Tennessee's pass defense fits what he does well. It ranks 26th in pass EPA allowed, 29th in explosive pass rate and 30th on short throws, and it gives up 289.9 passing yards a game to quarterbacks (31st). Lead receivers have feasted: WR1s score well above their usual output against it. Its deep defense is closer to average (18th), so the edge is more on timing throws and intermediate routes than on pure shots, which is his best zone anyway. The complication is the script. Jacksonville is a 10.5-point road favorite at -550, opponents lean on the run against Tennessee more than almost anyone, and the Titans' offense ranks 27th. A comfortable lead with the run game closing it out is the likeliest path, which is how he threw just 14 passes against Indianapolis.

Jacksonville has no offensive injuries listed, and he gets 10 days of rest after the Thursday game in Baltimore. On Tennessee's side, CB Marcus Harris (56% of snaps) is questionable with an ankle injury, which thins a secondary that is already struggling. Guard Peter Skoronski and tackle JC Latham are also questionable; those reports date to November 1. If they sit, Tennessee's offense gets worse and the blowout script becomes more likely: good for efficiency, bad for attempts. WR Carnell Tate being out does the same.

keyMatchups.title: Parker Washington against a WR1 sieve
keyMatchups.body: Washington leads the team in targets, and Tennessee has been one of the worst defenses in the league against opposing top receivers, both in fantasy points over their averages and in EPA per target. Wide receivers draw a larger share of targets against this defense than the league norm, while tight ends draw less. That points the volume outside and toward Washington and Meyers rather than Strange.

keyMatchups.title: Soft underneath, explosive-prone coverage
keyMatchups.body: Tennessee ranks 30th in EPA allowed on short throws and 29th in explosive pass rate. That lets Lawrence's short game, his weakest band, play up, and it gives his intermediate throws room to break into big gains. This is where an efficient day comes from even on limited attempts.

keyMatchups.title: Run-funnel game script
keyMatchups.body: Offenses run more against Tennessee than situation predicts, and a top-three Jaguars defense facing a bottom-six offense should produce an early lead. Expect Lawrence's attempts to sit at or below his season norm, so efficiency should carry the day more than volume.

nextGame.watch: Whether his CPOE rebounds against a soft secondary: a clean, accurate game would say the recent slide was noise; another negative mark in an easy matchup would be a warning.

restOfSeason.body:
The foundation looks durable: better ball placement, a quicker clock and an intermediate passing game that has worked against varied defenses. He should stay among the most efficient passers in the league. What will not hold is the touchdown rate. Red-zone finishing at sub-50% completion and a near-double league TD rate point to fewer scores, something closer to his strong 2025 pace than to the current 38-touchdown pace. Volume is the other limiter. A run-balanced offense and a top-three defense keep his attempts in the high 20s, so his yardage will track his efficiency rather than explode.

I'd project roughly 225-270 passing yards and 1.5-2.2 touchdowns a game, with rushing staying a minor contributor at 6-16 yards and fantasy output around 15-21 PPR points. The biggest swing is whether the accuracy that defined September returns or keeps sliding; next is how often the defense turns games into early blowouts.
swingFactors: Whether his CPOE recovers from the recent slide

confidence.note: Eight starts and a stable role, but a career-outlier TD rate and fading recent accuracy add uncertainty.
